newsitem.title: USA: Blue-chip stocks down for fourth straight day.
newsitem.headline: Blue-chip stocks down for fourth straight day.

text.p: Blue-chip stocks extended their sell-off into a fourth session Thursday amid weakness in bonds and a plunge in the shares of consumer products giant Procter & Gamble Co.
At 1 p.m. EDT, the Dow Jones industrial average was down 32.42 points at 6,004.04 -- 90 points off its last record high of 6,094.23 set on Friday.
In the broader market, declining issues beat advances 12-9 on active volume of 228 million shares on the New York Stock Exchange.
The Nasdaq Composite index gained 3.08 points at 1,230.96, as technology stocks extended their recovery into a second day. The American Stock Exchange index was down 1.28 at 569.45.
In the bond market, the benchmark 30-year bond was down 14/32, raising its yield to 6.87 percent from 6.83 percent on Wednesday.
The bond market sold off on smaller-than-expected weekly jobless claims of 320,000 vs. Wall Street's expectations for 336,000, indicating the economy was more robust than had been anticipated.

"Bonds are unhappy about the strong employment statistics which, combined with better retail activity as expressed in same store sales over the past few weeks, seem to be indicating that the economy in the fourth quarter will be stronger than it was in the third quarter," said Peter Canelo, chief investment strategist at Dean Witter.
"Things are not slowing down," he said. "In the long run, this means better earnings which is something the market will benefit from."
Canelo said bond traders worried about how the Federal Reserve, which has held off so far from raising interest rates to slow growth, may react to the economic data.
He said that the stock market has had a good run and that the concerns now arising were essentially an opportunity for investors to take profits.
The 30-stock Dow index was pressured by a drop in Procter & Gamble, which tumbled 3-1/2 to 92-3/4 after reporting fiscal first quarter results.

P&G said its profits rose by 9 percent to a record $979 million in the latest quarter but its revenues slipped to $8.90 billion from $9.03 billion due to the impact of a strong dollar on overseas sales.
Gregory Nie, technical analyst at Everen Securities, said the stock market was beginning to show wear and tear, which was evident in diminishing trading volumes compared with earlier this year.
"The volume level is not the same as it was earlier in the year. That comes from pushing to new highs" he said. "We don't seem to be able to create robust volume on the upside."
He said there was a lack of investment demand.
"I think we are looking at the end of an up-phase to be followed by a minor move down to work off the overbought condition," Nie said.
Among special situations, Dell Computer Corp. was up 2-1/2 at 85 after Merrill Lynch raised its 1997 earnings per share estimate for the company.
In the high technology sector, Microsoft Corp. rose 2-1/4 at 136-3/4 and Intel Corp. was up 1 at 110-3/8.
